answer: To resist sybil attacks, each agent must periodically publish a unique computational beacon derived from a private basalt seed that encodes recent interaction history. Peers issue random challenges that the agent must echo by recomputing a hash chain segment tied to that beacon within a short window. An attacker spinning many fake identities faces multiplicative compute costs because each clone needs its own continuous beacon maintenance and rapid echo responses, making large-scale sybil farms economically unviable compared to honest single agents.
